messages:
maria: quick heads-up — ran a 20k-token long-context run on hosted vs dedicated vs private and saw divergent kv residency patterns :thinking_face:
ajay: rough numbers?
kelly: did you use the same model+quant profile across all three? small config drift can blow up kv behavior
maria: same model (llama-13b), same quant, pinned model version. differences were infra-level: hosted uses our shared host kernel 6.x + container runtime A, dedicated uses locked-down nodes with kernel 5.15 and newer nvidia driver, private onprem is ubuntu18 + older driver + 2x A100s in NVLink
perf-bot: perf dashboard: https://console.redwood/perf/dash/kv-residency-185867 — shows memory ladder and pagefault spike at ~14k tokens :eyes:
dave: spike at 14k sounds like kv page reclamation kicking in — logs?
maria: pasted snippet from the profiler:
```
kv_cache: total_bytes=42.1G resident=28.4G swapped=13.7G
page_faults: major=0 minor=4.2k
eviction_ops: small_chunks=12.3k fragmented_bytes=1.6G
longest_kv_ttl=3.1s
```
kelly: hosted shows higher swapped bytes? that implies our shared host cgroup memory + swap config is allowing pageout. Dedicated had much lower swapped and lower fragmentation
ajay: on private, we saw a weird pattern: resident stayed high but reuse dropped — meaning lots of pages kept around but not reused, i.e., fragmentation + false locality
lucy: could be NUMA pinning differences on onprem. are theCUDA allocations pinned to a single NUMA node? that can make device-to-host copies different and change cache eviction timings
maria: confirmed NUMA mismatch on private: job pinned to numa0 but process touched memory across nodes. We also had cgroup memory.high at 75% on hosted which allowed more swapping
dave: another factor: kernel selection for attention kernels. Hosted fell back to a lower-latency kernel earlier because of observed tail latencies — that reduces in-flight batch size which affects prefix reuse and kv cache hit rate
elly: (typo) meant kelly
kelly: good catch — batch heuristic config differs by env: hosted uses latency-first policy (max_batch=4, timeout=10ms), dedicated uses throughput-first (max_batch=12, timeout=40ms). Smaller batches -> less KV reuse -> more churn -> more small evicts
ajay: so config drift + kernel fallback + NUMA/drivers = composite effect. Any repro steps people can run locally?
maria: minimal repro script I used:
```
# run 1: hosted-like
REDWOOD_KV_MAX=45G REDWOOD_BATCH_POLICY=latency python perf_run.py --context 20000
# run 2: dedicated-like
REDWOOD_KV_MAX=45G REDWOOD_BATCH_POLICY=throughput python perf_run.py --context 20000
```
lucy: for onprem add: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 numactl --cpunodebind=0 --membind=0 to mimic the mismatch
dave: suggestion — add an agent that emits kv residency hist per-token and a flag when the runtime falls back kernels. we can correlate fallback events with eviction spikes
kelly: +1. Also add a guard: if fragmented_bytes/total > 0.05 then trigger compacting pass (cheap) or promote larger-slot allocations
ajay: watch out — compacting pass is expensive during long contexts. maybe schedule it during idle windows or when SLO headroom is available
maria: noted. I'll open a small RFC tomorrow: suggested fixes = (1) unify batch policy templates across envs for long-context workloads, (2) NUMA-aware device binding in onprem package, (3) telemetry for kernel-fallback -> eviction correlation, (4) a low-cost fragmentation monitor and adaptive compact/evict policy
perf-bot: created ticket PERF-1249: kv-residency telemetry + adaptive compacting (https://issues.redwood/PERF-1249) :thumbsup:
lucy: can we include driver/kernel matrix in the ticket so infra knows which nodes to repro on
maria: yes — I'll attach node manifests and the profiler flamegraphs. thanks team :raised_hands:
